Two simulations are carried out on this problem, both with the AP-Moment scheme (note that the Gauss elliptic correction is not implemented in these simulations). The plasma and discretization parameters are specified in Table 2. The evolution of the magnetic field for the simulation (a), reported in Figure 7, shows a rapid magnetization of the plasma in the region where the density gradient is located. The electrons emitted at the cathode produce a current which prevents a uniform penetration of the magnetic field in the plasma. This current is gradually deflected with the propagation of the magnetic field, as depicted in Figures 7(c) and 7(d). We evaluate the speed of the KMC waves in the simulations by marking the position of a certain magnetic level set at different times (see Figure 8). The observed values are in agreement with the theoretical values: in the simulation (a), it is 76% of the theoretical value, while in the simulation (b), it reaches 82% of the theoretical value. These good numerical results are obtained with discretizations that do not resolve the Debye length. In particular, for the discretization (a), the mesh size is 10410^{4} times larger than the Debye length.

6 Conclusion

We have derived two Asymptotic-Preserving Particle-In-Cell methods for the Vlasov-Maxwell system in the quasi-neutral limit. The scaling assumptions made for the definition of the quasi-neutral limit, similar to those used to derive the MHD models, yield a kinetic quasi-neutral model where the electric field is computed by means of a generalized Ohm law. The Asymptotic-Preserving methods are consistent with either the quasi-neutral model or the Vlasov-Maxwell model according to how the discretization parameters resolve the plasma parameters, which make them able to simulate complex plasma problems with a reasonable computational cost. No rigorous numerical analysis is provided in this article and this should be the subject of future work. However, the numerous numerical investigations demonstrate conclusively the efficiency of the methods to account for phenomena evolving at the plasma period and Debye length scales, as well as quasi-neutral phenomena usually well described by the MHD theory. In particular, they are able to cope with vacuum-dense plasma interfaces and the formation of non-neutral sheaths. Although other semi-implicit Particle-In-Cell methods (the Direct Implicit and Implicit Moment methods) present the same kind of Asymptotic-Preserving properties, the methodology developed in this article is new and provides a rigorous framework for the quasi-neutral limit problem. Furthermore, it opens the way for addressing more singular asymptotics and deriving more efficient numerical methods for some kinds of problems.

Appendix A Yee finite differences and θ\theta-scheme for the Maxwell equations

We consider the discretization of the homogeneous dd-dimensional Maxwell equations (d=d=1, 2 or 3) with Yee finite differences for the space approximation and a θ\theta-scheme for the time integration. Using the discrete operators introduced in Section 3.1, the discrete equations are

1c2​Ehm+1−EhmΔ​t−∇h×B¯hm+θ=0,\displaystyle\frac{1}{c^{2}}\frac{E^{m+1}_{h}-E^{m}_{h}}{\Delta t}-\nabla_{h}\times\bar{B}^{m+\theta}_{h}=0\,, (119)
Bhm+1−BhmΔ​t+∇h×E¯hm+θ=0,\displaystyle\frac{B^{m+1}_{h}-B^{m}_{h}}{\Delta t}+\nabla_{h}\times\bar{E}^{m+\theta}_{h}=0\,, (120)

with

E¯hm+θ=θ​Ehm+1+(1−θ)​Ehm,B¯hm+θ=θ​Bhm+1+(1−θ)​Bhm.\bar{E}^{m+\theta}_{h}=\theta E^{m+1}_{h}+(1-\theta)E^{m}_{h}\,,\qquad\bar{B}^{m+\theta}_{h}=\theta B^{m+1}_{h}+(1-\theta){B}^{m}_{h}\,.

The above scheme is second-order accurate in space. It is first-order accurate in time for θ≠12\theta\neq\frac{1}{2} and second-order accurate for θ=12\theta=\frac{1}{2}. The following energy balance holds true:

ℰhm+1−ℰhm=−(θ−12)​(ϵ0​(Ehm+1−Ehm)2+1μ0​(Bhm+1−Bhm)2),\mathcal{E}_{h}^{m+1}-\mathcal{E}_{h}^{m}=-\left(\theta-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(\epsilon_{0}\left(E^{m+1}_{h}-E^{m}_{h}\right)^{2}+\frac{1}{\mu_{0}}\left(B^{m+1}_{h}-B^{m}_{h}\right)^{2}\right)\,, (121)

where ℰhm=ϵ02​‖Ehm‖2+12​μ0​‖Bhm‖2\mathcal{E}_{h}^{m}=\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{2}\|E^{m}_{h}\|^{2}+\frac{1}{2\mu_{0}}\|B^{m}_{h}\|^{2}. Therefore, the θ\theta-scheme is unconditionally stable for θ∈[12,1]\theta\in[\frac{1}{2},1]. It is dissipative for θ∈]12,1]\theta\in]\frac{1}{2},1] (all the more dissipative than θ\theta is large) and energy-conserving for θ=12\theta=\frac{1}{2}. Unlike the leap-frog scheme, the θ\theta-scheme is dispersive even in a one-dimensional setting and with a Courant number equal to 1.

Appendix B Comparison of some particle pushers for the AP schemes

We examine the properties of some particle pushers within the AP schemes. The particle pushers we consider are variants of the Boris scheme:

XN,jm+1−XN,jmΔ​t=VN,jm+b,\displaystyle\frac{X_{N,j}^{m+1}-X_{N,j}^{m}}{\Delta t}=V_{N,j}^{m+b}\,, (122)
VN,jm+1−VN,jmΔ​t=−Ehm+c​(XN,jm+a)−VN,j++VN,j−2×Bhm​(XN,jm),\displaystyle\frac{V_{N,j}^{m+1}-V_{N,j}^{m}}{\Delta t}=-E_{h}^{m+c}(X_{N,j}^{m+a})-\frac{V_{N,j}^{+}+V_{N,j}^{-}}{2}\times B_{h}^{m}(X_{N,j}^{m})\,, (123)
VN,j+=VN,jm+1−12​Δ​t​Ehm​(XN,jm),\displaystyle V_{N,j}^{+}=V_{N,j}^{m+1}-\frac{1}{2}\Delta tE^{m}_{h}\left(X_{N,j}^{m}\right)\,, (124)
VN,j−=VN,jm+12​Δ​t​Ehm​(XN,jm),\displaystyle V_{N,j}^{-}=V_{N,j}^{m}+\frac{1}{2}\Delta tE^{m}_{h}\left(X_{N,j}^{m}\right)\,, (125)

with (a,b,c)∈{0,1}3(a,b,c)\in\{0,1\}^{3}.

Numerical simulations show that the electric field and the velocity must be made implicit (b=1b=1, c=1c=1) to overcome the stability condition (72). They also show that, whatever the choice for (a,b,c)(a,b,c), the scheme remains subject to the Courant condition (74). An explicit discretization of the position (a=0a=0) is preferable to an implicit discretization (a=1a=1), since it yields a scheme easier to solve and more accurate. In particular, in the case of a constant electric field and a zero magnetic field, the choice a=0a=0 yields a symplectic scheme, unlike the choice a=1a=1. Symplectic time-integration schemes ensure excellent conservation properties and an accurate behavior in long-time simulations [29].

Appendix C KMC waves

The existence of KMC waves can be derived from the quasi-neutral equations (with motionless ions) presented in Section 2.3. Neglecting the inertia term ∂tJ\partial_{t}J and the pressure term ∇⋅S\nabla\cdot S in the generalized Ohm law (25) and rewriting it with dimensional variables, we obtain the relation

n​E−1e​J×B=0nE-\frac{1}{e}J\times B=0

Then, using the Maxwell-Ampère equation and Maxwell-Faraday equations (still with dimensional variables), we deduce that the magnetic field evolution is governed only by the Hall term:

∂tB=−∇×((∇×B×B)/(μ0en)).\partial_{t}B=-\nabla\times\big(({\nabla\times B\times B)/(\mu_{0}en})\big)\,.

In the two-dimensional setting (116)-(117), if the density does not vary along the xx-axis and does vary along the yy-axis, the above equation simplifies into a Burgers-like nonlinear hyperbolic equation:

∂tBz=−12​e​μ0∂y(1n)∂xBz2.\partial_{t}B_{z}=-\frac{1}{2e\mu_{0}}\partial_{y}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\partial_{x}B_{z}^{2}\,.

This equation admits shock wave solutions, with a speed

V=Bze​μ0​∂y(1n).V=\frac{B_{z}}{e\mu_{0}}\partial_{y}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\,. (126)

They are the so-called KMC waves, named after Kingsep, Mokhov and Chukbar.
